# The Vermillion Seal

In the eighteenth year of Emperor Xuanzong's reign, during the height of the Tang Dynasty, there lived a scholar named Wei Chen in the southern province of Guangdong. He was a man of modest means but considerable learning, traveling to the capital city of Chang'an to sit for the imperial examinations.

The journey was long, and one autumn evening, Wei Chen found himself far from any town as darkness fell. A cold mist rose from the rice paddies, and the moon hung pale and distant behind gathering clouds. Just as he resigned himself to sleeping beneath the stars, he spotted a flicker of light through the fog—a grand estate with vermillion-painted gates.

Grateful for his fortune, Wei Chen approached and knocked. The gate swung open silently, though he saw no servant. The courtyard beyond was magnificent: stone lions guarded the entrance, and a reflecting pool held perfectly still water despite the evening breeze. Lanterns hung from the eaves, casting dancing shadows across the tiles.

"Welcome, Scholar Wei," came a melodious voice.

He turned to see a young woman of extraordinary beauty, dressed in robes of jade-green silk embroidered with silver phoenixes. Her face was powdered white, her lips painted crimson, and her hair was arranged in the elaborate style of the previous dynasty.

"You know my name?" Wei Chen asked, bowing respectfully.

"We have been expecting you," she said, her smile not quite reaching her eyes. "I am Lady Mei. My father, the magistrate, offers hospitality to all learned men. Please, you must be hungry."

Despite a strange unease creeping along his spine, Wei Chen's stomach growled, and he followed her into the main hall. The feast laid before him was magnificent—roasted duck, steamed fish, delicate dumplings, and wine that glowed golden in the lamplight. Yet as he ate, he noticed Lady Mei never touched her food, only watching him with dark, unblinking eyes.

"Your father is most generous," Wei Chen said. "Where is the magistrate? I should thank him personally."

"My father is... occupied with official matters," Lady Mei replied. "He asks that you stay the night. The guest chamber is prepared."

The wine had made Wei Chen drowsy, and he agreed. Lady Mei led him through winding corridors, past rooms filled with furniture covered in white cloth, to a chamber at the far end of the compound. The bed was soft, the linens clean, but the air smelled faintly of incense and something else—something like earth after heavy rain.

As he lay down, he noticed a small wooden plaque above the door, bearing characters in an archaic script. His scholarly training allowed him to read: "Here lies the devoted daughter of Magistrate Huang. May her spirit find peace."

Wei Chen's blood turned cold. He rose and examined the plaque more closely. The date of death was seventy years past.

A soft laugh echoed through the chamber. Lady Mei stood in the doorway, but now her beautiful face had become translucent, revealing the skull beneath. Her elegant robes hung on skeletal shoulders.

"You see truly, Scholar Wei," she said, her voice like wind through bamboo. "I have been dead these many decades. This estate burned to the ground during the rebellion, and everyone within perished. My father, the servants, and I—all consumed by flames."

Wei Chen pressed himself against the wall, but his scholarly composure held. "What do you want from me?" he managed to ask.

Lady Mei's ghostly form drifted closer. "Only what I wanted in life—to hear the words of poetry, to discuss philosophy, to know the world of learning that was denied to me. I was to be married to an official's son, but I died before the wedding. I have remained here, trapped, yearning for the scholarly discussions my father shared with his guests."

Her sadness was palpable, and despite his terror, Wei Chen felt pity stir in his chest. "If I stay and speak with you until dawn, will you let me go unharmed?"

"Yes," she whispered. "One night only. Tomorrow, you may leave."

And so, in that chamber between the world of the living and the dead, Wei Chen recited poetry from the masters—Li Bai, Du Fu, Wang Wei. He discussed the teachings of Confucius and Laozi. He shared stories from the imperial court and described the great capital he had seen.

Lady Mei listened with an expression of profound longing. As he spoke, color gradually returned to her cheeks, and her form became almost solid, as if his words were giving her temporary life.

But as the first cock crowed and dawn light touched the window, she began to fade once more.

"Thank you, Scholar Wei," she said, her voice growing distant. "In seventy years, only you have seen me as a person rather than a horror. For this kindness, I give you a gift."

She pressed something into his hand—a jade seal, carved with the character for "success."

"Show this when you reach the examination hall. It belonged to my father, a man of great integrity. It will bring you good fortune."

The light grew stronger, and Lady Mei vanished like mist in the sun. Wei Chen found himself standing not in a grand estate, but among ruins—burned timbers and crumbling walls, overtaken by weeds and wild vines. The jade seal was cool and solid in his palm, the only proof his night had been real.

He continued his journey to Chang'an, and when he presented the seal to the examination officials, an elderly minister recognized it immediately. It had indeed belonged to Magistrate Huang, a renowned and upright official who had died decades ago.

"This seal was lost in the rebellion," the minister said, eyes wide with wonder. "Where did you find it?"

Wei Chen told his story truthfully. Some scoffed, but the minister believed, for he had served under Magistrate Huang in his youth. "He had a daughter of remarkable intelligence," the old man confirmed. "It grieved him that she would never have the opportunity to pursue learning. You honored her memory, young scholar."

Whether through supernatural aid or his own merit, Wei Chen passed the examinations with the highest marks. He went on to become a respected official, known for his compassion and his unusual belief that women should be educated.

But every year on the anniversary of that night, he would burn incense and paper money for Lady Mei, the ghost who had sought not to harm, but simply to learn. And sometimes, in his dreams, he would see her smiling—truly smiling—as she finally faded into whatever peace awaited her beyond the veil.

The jade seal remained in his family for generations, a reminder that even the dead may yearn for nothing more than to be treated with dignity and understanding.

---

*And so the story was recorded in the annals of strange tales, a reminder to travelers in ancient China to show respect to all spirits, for not all ghosts seek vengeance—some seek only what they were denied in life.*
